newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Army strikes said pushing Angola toward volatility.
newsitem.headline: Army strikes said pushing Angola toward volatility.

text.p: A respected former advisor to Angola's former rebel UNITA movement said on Tuesday the country's main factions were preparing for military battles despite a 30-month-old peace treaty.

But Sean Cleary, who now heads a top risk management company in Johannesburg, ruled out a return of a full-scale war in Angola, saying the collapse of a cooperative civil and economic framework built under the peace agreement was the greater danger.

"I don't think war is seriously a prospect for Angola. The risk is if you don't get reconciliation on the leadership level, then we will see the collapse of the framework of the Lusaka Protocol," he told a meeting of the South African Institute of International Affairs.
He said UNITA's 62-year-old leader Jonas Savimbi had no inclination to resume its 20-year civil war against the government, headed by President Jose Eduardo dos Santos.
Cleary also said UNITA was not under any illusion that it had the resources to win on the battlefield.

A month-old Angolan army offensive in the diamond-rich northeast had, however, prompted UNITA to reactivate some of its former military bases and mobilise its forces in the central province of Uige, Cleary said.
He said UNITA was also being helped by former Zairean soldiers once loyal to ousted president Mobutu Sese Seko, a close ally of Savimbi's. He gave no details, however.

Angola's national army has taken control of at least 10 UNITA-held diamond-mining districts in the last month, saying it is acting to curtail an influx of former Zairean refugees flooding the northern border.
It has met resistance from heavily armed UNITA members protecting the movement's mining interests which some industry analysts put as high as 80 percent of all diamond territory in the country.

Cleary said government forces were now preparing for an assault in the central provinces. He said they had removed tanks, artillery pieces and armoured personnel carriers from underground bunkers at a commando training base and transferred them to an area close to Angola's second capital, Huambo.

"It is clear that both sides are positioning for a new round of fighting. This will not begin before the meeting of the U.N. Security Council, scheduled for June 27, and will probably commence -- if not checked before then -- only in the second or third week of July," Cleary said.
"The wind is now set firmly for a new clash."
The United Nations special envoy to Angola, Alioune Blondin Beye, left Luanda for New York on Monday to brief the U.N. Security Council on Angola's peace process.
Cleary said the Security Council session might spur a long overdue meeting between dos Santos and Savimbi "before the die is cast", to avert prolonged fighting.
"The only possibility of avoiding another costly conflagration is still a meeting -- and an understanding -- between President dos Santos and Dr Savimbi," he said.

"The question is simply whether Angola's present leaders have the wisdom and courage to sidestep this looming disaster, or whether the country will be condemned to one more round of bloodletting before sense prevails."
